questions.question: How are the six faces of the plot die divided?
choices: Two blank, two Opportunity, two Complication
Three blank, two Opportunity, one Complication
One blank, three Opportunity, two Complication
Two blank, one Opportunity, three Complication
questions.explanation: The plot die is split evenly: two blank faces, two Opportunity faces and two Complication faces. On a normal d6 stand-in, 1–2 are Complications, 3–4 blank, 5–6 Opportunities.

questions.question: When the plot die comes up as a Complication, what upside does the roller get?
choices: Nothing — a Complication is purely a drawback
Add the number on the symbol (+2 or +4) to the roll
They may reroll the plot die once for free
They recover 1 focus to offset the setback
questions.explanation: A plot-die Complication also adds a bonus equal to the number on the symbol (+2 or +4) to the current d20 roll, so a Complication can actually help the test succeed.

questions.question: Which statement about raising the stakes is correct?
choices: The GM may raise them after seeing the d20 result
They can be raised twice on a critical test
Once per test, and only before the d20 is rolled
Only players may raise them; the GM just approves
questions.explanation: Raising the stakes happens once per test at most, and it must be decided before the d20 is rolled — never after.

questions.question: A natural 1 on the d20 gives a Complication. How does it differ from a plot-die Complication?
choices: It grants no bonus to the test
It grants a +4 bonus instead of +2
It automatically fails the test
It cannot be spent by the GM
questions.explanation: Complications from the d20's Complication range (a natural 1 by default) don't come with the +2/+4 bonus that plot-die Complications provide.

questions.question: A talent expands your Opportunity range by 2 for a skill. Which natural d20 results now grant an Opportunity on that skill?
choices: 20 only
20–22 (i.e. you need 2 less on the die)
questions.explanation: Expanding the Opportunity range lowers its starting number. The default range is 20 alone, so expanding it by 2 makes it 18 through 20.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the standard ways to spend an Opportunity?
choices: Give an ally's next test an advantage
Recover 1 focus
Turn a hit into a critical hit on an attack test
Recover 1 Investiture
questions.explanation: The standard Opportunity spends are Aid an Ally (advantage on an ally's next test), Collect Yourself (recover 1 focus), Critically Hit (attack tests only) and Influence the Narrative. Recovering Investiture isn't one of them.

questions.question: Which of these is one of the GM's standard ways to spend a Complication?
choices: The roller takes 1d4 impact damage
The next test made by a PC gains a disadvantage
The roller loses their next reaction this round
The roller loses 1 Investiture or 1 health
questions.explanation: The standard Complication spends are Hinder an Ally (the next PC test gains a disadvantage), Become Distracted (lose 1 focus) and Influence the Narrative.

questions.question: Do NPCs normally roll the plot die on their tests?
choices: Yes, whenever a PC would
Only bosses and Fused
Generally no
Only when a PC raises the stakes against them
questions.explanation: The plot die is a tool for PC tests during tense moments; NPC tests generally don't use it.

questions.question: An ability lets a character with a 25-foot movement rate move half their movement. How far can they move?
choices: 12 feet
12.5 feet
13 feet
15 feet
questions.explanation: Unless a rule says otherwise, you always round down when dividing, so half of 25 is 12.

questions.question: As a general rule, when do two similar effects NOT stack on the same target?
choices: When they come from the same character
When they share the same name
When they both grant bonuses to defenses
When either one has a duration
questions.explanation: Similar effects generally stack unless they share the same name.

questions.question: A talent's text contradicts a general rule in the core mechanics. Which applies?
choices: The general rule, since it's foundational
The talent's specific rule
Whichever is more favorable to the PC
Neither — the GM must make a skill test
questions.explanation: Specific beats general: when a talent, power or item contradicts a general rule, the specific rule wins (and the GM has final say on any uncertainty).

questions.question: Normally, how many reactions can a character use between each of their turns?
choices: None
One
Two
As many as they have focus for
questions.explanation: A character typically gets one reaction between each of their turns, used when a specific trigger occurs.

questions.question: The stakes are raised on a PC's Athletics test. They roll a natural 20 on the d20 and an Opportunity on the plot die. What do they get?
choices: One Opportunity — duplicates merge
Two Opportunities
One Opportunity plus a +4 bonus
A critical success, which replaces Opportunities
questions.explanation: A natural 20 grants an Opportunity even when the plot die is also rolled, so the PC can end up with two Opportunities on the same test.

questions.question: A PC with an advantage rolls two d20s for a Stealth test and gets a 1 and a 16. They use the 16. Do they gain a Complication?
choices: Yes — any natural 1 rolled adds a Complication
Yes, but it gives no +2/+4 bonus
No — only the d20 they chose can add one
No — an advantage cancels any Complication
questions.explanation: When rolling multiple d20s, a die only adds an Opportunity or Complication if its result is the one chosen for the test. The unused 1 has no effect.

cite.section: Introduction › Ranges When Rolling Multiple D20s

questions.question: A PC benefits from two effects with the same name, each saying it expands their Opportunity range by 2 on this test. Which natural rolls grant an Opportunity?
choices: 20 only
questions.explanation: Range expansions stack only when they come from effects with different names. Two same-named effects count once, so the range is 18–20.

questions.question: A player spends an Opportunity to influence the narrative, but you (the GM) think their proposed effect isn't possible. What do the rules say happens?
choices: The Opportunity is simply lost
The player must accept a Complication instead
You decide; agree on another effect or they pick a different one
The player rolls a d20 against DC 15 to force it through
questions.explanation: The GM has the final say on narrative Opportunity effects. If one isn't approved, the table can agree on a new narrative effect or the player can choose a different Opportunity effect.

questions.question: How is a character's Physical, Cognitive or Spiritual defense calculated?
choices: 10 + the higher attribute in that category
10 + both attributes in that category, plus modifiers
8 + both attributes in that category + their tier
12 + the lower attribute in that category + ranks
questions.explanation: Each defense is 10 plus both attributes of its category (e.g. Strength and Speed for Physical), plus any bonuses or penalties.

questions.question: At character creation, what is a character's maximum health?
choices: 10 + Strength
10 + Strength + Speed
2 + Strength
20 + Strength
questions.explanation: Starting maximum health is 10 plus Strength (plus any bonuses or penalties); it then grows with levels per the Character Advancement table.

questions.question: What is a character's maximum focus?
choices: 2 + Intellect
2 + Willpower
10 + Willpower
Willpower + Intellect
questions.explanation: Maximum focus equals 2 plus Willpower, plus any bonuses or penalties.

questions.question: Once a character gains an Investiture pool from a Radiant path, what is their maximum Investiture?
choices: 2 + Willpower, like focus
2 + Awareness + Presence combined
2 + the higher of Awareness or Presence
Equal to their current maximum focus
questions.explanation: Maximum Investiture is 2 plus whichever of Awareness or Presence is higher, plus any bonuses or penalties. New characters start with no Investiture.

questions.question: Which damage types does a character's deflect value reduce?
choices: All damage types
Impact, keen and energy
Impact and keen only
Keen, energy and spirit
questions.explanation: Deflect (usually from armor) reduces impact, keen and energy damage by the deflect value. Other damage types bypass it.

questions.question: A character with Speed 3 uses the Move action. What is their movement rate?
choices: 25 feet per action
30 feet per action
35 feet per action
40 feet per action
questions.explanation: On the Movement Rate table, Speed 3–4 gives 30 feet per action (Speed 1–2 is 25 feet, 5–6 is 40 feet).

questions.question: Which attribute determines the size of a character's recovery die?
choices: Strength
Willpower
Awareness
Presence
questions.explanation: Willpower sets the recovery die, from 1d4 at Willpower 0 up through 1d6, 1d8, 1d10 and 1d12, to 1d20 at Willpower 9+.

questions.question: A character with Awareness 3 has their primary sense obscured. How far is their senses range?
choices: 5 feet
10 feet
20 feet
50 feet
questions.explanation: On the Senses Range table, Awareness 3–4 gives 20 feet (1–2 is 10 feet, 5–6 is 50 feet).

questions.question: What happens if a character moves while carrying more than their carrying capacity?
choices: They can't move at all until they drop items
They're Slowed; after 60 total minutes, Exhausted [−1]
They take 1d4 impact damage each round they move
They gain a disadvantage on all physical tests
questions.explanation: Moving while over carrying capacity makes you Slowed. Each cumulative 60 minutes spent over capacity also makes you Exhausted [−1]; the cumulative time resets after a long rest.

questions.question: How can a character gain a specialist expertise (such as Shardblades or Fabrial Crafting)?
choices: By choosing it with a point of Intellect
Only through a talent, a reward or GM permission
By spending downtime training, like any other expertise
Automatically on reaching tier 2
questions.explanation: Specialist expertises can't be chosen with the extra expertises from Intellect; they come only from a talent, a reward or GM permission.

questions.question: How many expertises does a new character start with (before talents and other sources)?
choices: Two cultural expertises plus one per point of Intellect
One cultural expertise plus one per point of Intellect
One per point of Intellect plus one per point of Willpower
Three expertises of any category, chosen freely
questions.explanation: Characters begin with two cultural expertises plus additional expertises equal to their Intellect score, and gain another each time Intellect rises by 1.

questions.question: How is a skill modifier calculated?
choices: Ranks in the skill × 2
Associated attribute + ranks in the skill
Associated attribute + the character's tier
10 + ranks in the skill
questions.explanation: Your skill modifier equals your score in the skill's associated attribute plus your ranks in that skill (0–5).

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Skill Ranks and Modifiers

questions.question: On the Difficulty Class Examples table, what DC represents a Hard task?
questions.explanation: The guideline DCs are Easy 10, Medium 15, Hard 20, Very Hard 25 and Nearly Impossible 30.

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Difficulty Class Examples

questions.question: In an opposed test, what happens when both characters tie?
choices: Both characters succeed at once
Reroll until one result is higher
Nobody meets the DC; it favors the status quo
The higher skill modifier wins the tie
questions.explanation: On a tie, neither side meets their DC. Both may fail, and in an aggressive contest the defender — the side trying to keep things the same — is favored.

questions.question: When an effect grants an automatic success on a test, what happens?
choices: Roll anyway; you can't fail but can gain Opportunities
No roll; you succeed with no Opportunity or Complication
You succeed and automatically gain one Opportunity
You roll only the plot die to see side effects
questions.explanation: With an automatic success you don't roll at all, so you get the benefits of success with no Opportunities or Complications.

questions.question: A PC has two advantages on an attack test. How are they applied?
choices: Roll three d20s together and keep the single best one
Roll two d20s, keep the best, and add +2 to the result
Each advantage doubles a different die; keep one of each pair
Both advantages must be applied to the d20, rolling three
questions.explanation: Each advantage picks a different die — the d20, the plot die or another die such as a damage die. You roll two of that die and keep one. The same die can't be chosen twice.

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Testing With Advantages

questions.question: When a PC tests with a disadvantage, who chooses which die is doubled and which result is kept?
choices: The player chooses both
The GM chooses both
The player chooses the die; the GM chooses the result
The GM chooses the die; the player chooses the result
questions.explanation: For each disadvantage, the GM picks which die is rolled twice and also picks which of the two results is kept.

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Testing With Disadvantages

questions.question: An enemy NPC makes a test with a disadvantage. Who chooses which of the doubled dice is kept?
choices: The GM
A player, typically the one whose character is most affected
The NPC always keeps the lower result automatically
Nobody — NPCs ignore disadvantages
questions.explanation: For enemy NPC tests the roles reverse: the GM picks for advantages, and a player (usually the most affected one) picks for disadvantages.

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Enemy NPC Tests

questions.question: A PC tries to intimidate a guard. By default, which of the guard's defenses sets the DC?
choices: Physical
Cognitive
Spiritual
The highest of the three
questions.explanation: A test against a character usually targets the defense in the same category as the skill. Intimidation is Willpower-based (cognitive), so it targets Cognitive defense.

questions.question: When the GM sets a DC by judgment, whose abilities should the task's difficulty be gauged against?
choices: The PC attempting the task
The party's average skill modifier
An average person, not a player character
The most capable NPC in the scene
questions.explanation: Difficulty is gauged by what an average humanoid could do, not a PC. A leap that's nearly impossible for an ordinary citizen is DC 30.

questions.question: A PC wearing armor with deflect 2 is hit for 7 keen damage. How much health do they lose?
choices: 0 — armor negates keen damage
questions.explanation: Deflect reduces keen, impact and energy damage by its value: 7 − 2 = 5 health lost.

questions.question: A PC's Lore test has two advantages (good research, a helpful archivist) and one disadvantage (time pressure). What do they roll?
choices: Two advantages and one disadvantage, each on a separate die
One advantage — the disadvantage cancels one advantage
Nothing extra — any disadvantage cancels all advantages
One disadvantage, because disadvantages take priority
questions.explanation: Advantages and disadvantages cancel one for one, so two advantages and one disadvantage leaves one advantage.

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Testing With Both

questions.question: A Windrunner Lashed a door shut with Adhesion. A PC tests Athletics against the Windrunner's Adhesion to force it open, and the results tie. What happens?
choices: The door opens — ties go to the active character
Both reroll
The door stays stuck — a tie favors the status quo
The GM decides with the plot die
questions.explanation: On a tie neither side meets their DC, and in an aggressive contest the result favors the defender, keeping things as they were. The door stays Lashed.

questions.question: A merchant with Spiritual defense 14 is already very friendly toward the party. A PC tests Persuasion. Which approach matches the rules?
choices: The DC must stay 14 — defenses are fixed
Lower the DC (e.g. to 11); you don't have to tell the player
Grant an advantage and announce it
Skip the test and grant an automatic success with an Opportunity
questions.explanation: The target's defense sets the base DC, but the GM may adjust it for circumstances. Unlike advantages and disadvantages, the GM doesn't have to reveal that change.

questions.question: A PC with the Thaylen cultural expertise wants to know the basic customs at a Thaylen merchant gathering. What should you do as GM?
choices: Call for a Lore test with an advantage
Call for an Insight test against DC 12
Just tell them — no test needed for basics
Call for a Lore test at DC 10
questions.explanation: Expertise means you automatically know the basic facts of that area — no Lore, Deduction or Insight test is needed for basics.

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Expertise Benefits (Assumed Knowledge)

questions.question: Outside combat, several characters work together on one task. How is it resolved by default?
choices: Everyone tests and the best result counts
Everyone tests and the average result counts
One leader tests, with an advantage per helper
One leader tests, with +2 per helper
questions.explanation: The person leading the effort makes a single test and gains one advantage per helper. Helpers must be able to reasonably do the task themselves; complex group tasks may become an endeavor instead.

questions.question: How does a character help an ally's test during combat?
choices: By spending 1 focus
By using the Aid reaction
By using the Gain Advantage action on the ally
They can't help in combat
questions.explanation: Helping in combat requires the Aid reaction; the 'one advantage per helper' rule is for working together outside combat.

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Helping in Combat

questions.question: An ability increases the die size of an attack that normally deals 1d4. What do you roll now?
questions.explanation: Increasing die size swaps the die for the next largest one: d4 → d6 → d8 → d10 → d12.

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Changing Die Size

questions.question: In general, what happens when you make a test to directly affect a character you can't sense (e.g. a surge or weapon attack)?
choices: The test automatically fails
You usually gain a disadvantage
The target gains +5 to its defenses
Nothing, as long as you know where they are
questions.explanation: If you can't sense a character, you usually gain a disadvantage on tests made to directly affect them.

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Targeting From a Distance

questions.question: A PC tries to deceive someone by letter. What's the rule?
choices: Deception simply can't be used at a distance at all
Disadvantage on Deception if they can't sense you
Test Lore instead, since the lie is in writing
Test Deception normally, but the DC increases by 5
questions.explanation: Long-distance deception (spanreed, letters, messengers) is harder: you test Deception with a disadvantage if the target can't sense you.

questions.question: Without making a test, how far can a moving character generally jump?
choices: 5 feet in any direction
Across: their size. Up: half their size
Across: half their movement rate
Across: 10 feet. Up: 3 feet
questions.explanation: A moving character can jump a horizontal distance equal to their size and a vertical distance equal to half their size without a test. Longer jumps need an Athletics test.

questions.question: What's needed to treat a conscious ally with Medicine during combat?
choices: A healing kit and 1 action, with no test
1+ Medicine rank, 2 focus, Use a Skill, DC 15 test
Any character, a reaction, and a DC 10 Medicine test
3 actions, a healing kit and a DC 20 Medicine test
questions.explanation: With at least 1 rank in Medicine, you spend 2 focus and Use a Skill for a DC 15 test on a conscious ally within reach (yourself with a disadvantage). On a success they recover health equal to your Medicine ranks.

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Medicine (Using Medicine in Combat)

questions.question: During a long rest, what does a successful DC 20 Medicine test on an injured ally do?
choices: Removes the injury entirely
Cuts a shallow or vicious injury by 1d4 days
Restores health equal to their Medicine ranks
Turns a vicious injury into a shallow one
questions.explanation: Treating an injury during a long rest (DC 20; with a disadvantage on yourself) cuts a shallow or vicious injury's duration by 1d4 days. Each character can only be treated this way once per long rest.

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Medicine (Using Medicine While Resting)

questions.question: In combat, what must be true for a character to attempt to hide from someone?
choices: They must be at least 30 feet from the target
Cover, obscured senses, or no line of effect
They must spend 1 focus and the Brace action
They must not have attacked this round
questions.explanation: Hiding in combat (Use a Skill: Stealth vs. Spiritual defense) requires cover, an area obscuring the target's primary sense (like darkness), or no line of effect to the target.

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Stealth (Hiding in Combat)

questions.question: When a hiding character tests Stealth in combat, which defense of the searcher do they test against?
choices: Physical
Cognitive
Spiritual
None — it's always an opposed Perception test
questions.explanation: Hiding in combat is a Stealth test against each character's Spiritual defense. Anyone you beat loses track of you.

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Stealth (Hiding in Combat)

questions.question: Which is true about pickpocketing in combat with Thievery?
choices: It's a free action with no test needed
Stakes raised; vs. Spiritual; disadvantage if they're aware
It targets Physical defense with an advantage
It only works against Unconscious or Surprised targets
questions.explanation: Pickpocketing in combat uses Use a Skill against a target within reach. You always raise the stakes, the DC is their Spiritual defense, and you gain a disadvantage if they're aware of your presence.

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Thievery (Pickpocketing in Combat)

questions.question: What does a character give up to forage with Survival during a short rest?
choices: Nothing — they still recover normally
The other benefits of resting
1 focus from their current pool
Their next reaction in the following scene
questions.explanation: Foraging during a short rest means giving up that rest's normal benefits to test Survival and collect resources.

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Survival (Foraging in Nature)

questions.question: A visibly sick PC who can barely stand threatens a thug by claiming to be a fearsome warrior. How does that affect the Intimidation test?
choices: No effect — bluffing never matters
The test gains a disadvantage
The test is impossible
Use Deception instead, with an advantage
questions.explanation: Plausible exaggeration doesn't change the test, but an obviously preposterous threat gives a disadvantage on the Intimidation test.

questions.question: What does a character need before they can make a Crafting test to build a weapon, armor or a fabrial?
choices: Nothing beyond a rank in Crafting
A corresponding expertise
A specialist workshop and 3 ranks
Intellect 3 or higher
questions.explanation: Commonplace items just need a Crafting test, but complex items like weapons, armor, equipment, grand works of art and fabrials need a corresponding expertise.

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Crafting (Crafting Complex Items)

questions.question: Outside combat, a PC leads an effort to decipher an enemy fabrial. Three allies want to help, but one lacks the Fabrial Crafting expertise the task needs. How many advantages does the leader get?
choices: 0 — the leader must roll alone
questions.explanation: Each helper grants one advantage, but helpers must be able to reasonably do the task themselves. The ally without the required expertise can't contribute, so the leader gets 2.

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Helping Outside Combat

questions.question: Mid-combat, a PC with 2 ranks in Medicine treats a wounded, conscious ally beside them and succeeds on the DC 15 test. What did it cost, and how much health does the ally recover?
choices: 1 action; the ally recovers 1d6
2 focus + Use a Skill; the ally recovers 2
2 focus; the ally recovers 2d4
No extra cost; the ally recovers 4
questions.explanation: Medicine in combat costs 2 focus and the Use a Skill action, and heals health equal to the healer's Medicine ranks — 2 here.

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Medicine (Using Medicine in Combat)

questions.question: A PC ducks behind crates and tests Stealth to hide from two guards, rolling a total of 17. Guard A has Spiritual defense 15; Guard B has 18. What's the result?
choices: Hidden from both — beat the lower defense
Hidden from neither — must beat both
Hidden from Guard A only
Hidden from Guard B only
questions.explanation: Compare the one Stealth result to each character's Spiritual defense. 17 beats Guard A's 15 but not Guard B's 18, so only Guard A loses track of the PC.

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Stealth (Hiding in Combat)

questions.question: A PC hid in a dark corridor with a Stealth result of 19. On his turn, a guard searches with Perception. What's the DC, and does anything modify his roll?
choices: DC 15, no modifier
His Spiritual defense, with an advantage
DC 19, with a disadvantage for him
DC 19, with no modifier
questions.explanation: A searcher uses Use a Skill for a Perception test whose DC is the hider's original Stealth result (19). They have a disadvantage if the hider is in cover or in an area obscuring the searcher's primary sense, like darkness.

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Stealth (Hiding in Combat)

questions.question: During a long rest, the party medic tries to shorten a companion's vicious injury but fails the Medicine test. Another PC with Medicine wants to try too. Can they?
choices: Yes, with an advantage from the first attempt
Yes, but the DC rises to 25 for a second try
No — only one treatment per long rest, success or not
Only if the second medic spends 2 focus first
questions.explanation: Once a character has been treated during a long rest, successfully or not, they can't be treated that way again until the next long rest.

cite.section: Ch. 3 Character Statistics › Medicine (Using Medicine While Resting)

questions.question: What does the Determined condition let you do?
choices: Gain an advantage on your next test
Add an Opportunity to a failed test, then it ends
Ignore the next Complication you would face
Reroll one failed test, then it ends
questions.explanation: While Determined, you can add an Opportunity to a failed test. Doing so removes the condition.

questions.question: Which set of effects describes the Disoriented condition?
choices: Movement halved; melee attacks vs. you gain an advantage
No reactions; senses obscured; disadvantage to Perception
You gain two fewer actions on your turn
Disadvantage on all tests except to escape
questions.explanation: Disoriented means you can't use reactions, your senses always count as obscured, and Perception (and similar sensing tests) gain a disadvantage.

questions.question: A Radiant becomes Empowered after swearing an Ideal. What does that grant, and when does it end?
choices: +2 to every test they make until their next long rest
Advantage on all tests and full Investiture each turn; ends with the scene
Double their maximum Investiture until the end of the round
Immunity to all damage until the end of their next turn
questions.explanation: Empowered grants an advantage on all tests and refills Investiture to maximum at the start of each of your turns. It's removed at the end of the current scene.

questions.question: Which is true of a Prone character?
choices: Ranged attacks against them gain an advantage
Slowed, and melee attacks vs. them gain an advantage
They can't take any actions until they stand
They are Immobilized and can't be moved
questions.explanation: While Prone you're Slowed and melee attacks against you gain an advantage. You can Brace without cover, and after standing up your movement rate is reduced by 5 until the start of your next turn.

questions.question: What does the Restrained condition do?
choices: Movement 0; disadvantage except to escape
Movement 0 only — tests are unaffected
Movement halved and no reactions
You can't move or be moved by other effects
questions.explanation: Restrained sets your movement rate to 0 and gives a disadvantage on all tests other than escaping your bonds. (Immobilized is the one that also stops other effects moving you.)

questions.question: A character becomes Enhanced [+2 Strength]. Which of these does NOT change?
choices: Athletics test results
Heavy Weaponry test results
Physical defense and maximum health
Talents that directly use Strength
questions.explanation: Enhanced boosts the attribute for skills, talents and things like movement, but explicitly doesn't change defenses, maximum health, maximum focus or maximum Investiture.

questions.question: How does the Exhausted condition go away?
choices: It ends automatically at the end of the scene
Each long rest reduces it by 1 until it reaches 0
A short rest removes it entirely
A successful DC 15 Discipline test ends it
questions.explanation: Each long rest reduces your Exhausted penalty by 1, and the condition is removed when the penalty reaches 0. Multiple instances add together.

questions.question: What does the Focused condition do?
choices: Grants an advantage on Discipline tests
Reduces the focus cost of your abilities by 1
Restores 1 focus per round
Prevents you from losing focus
questions.explanation: While Focused, abilities that cost focus cost 1 less.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT an effect of the Surprised condition?
choices: You lose any reactions you have
You can't take a fast turn
You gain one fewer action on your turn
Attacks vs. you become critical hits
questions.explanation: Surprised removes your reactions, stops you gaining a reaction at the start of combat or on your turn, bars fast turns, and costs you one action. It ends after your next turn. Nothing makes attacks auto-crit.

questions.question: Can a character be Afflicted by more than one effect at the same time?
choices: No — only the strongest applies
Yes — resolve each effect separately
Yes, but only two at once
Only if they're different damage types
questions.explanation: Unlike most conditions, you can be Afflicted by several effects at once, resolving each separately. In combat, the damage happens at the end of each of your turns.

questions.question: When can an Unconscious PC choose to wake up?
choices: Only when another character heals them
At the end of any of their turns, or when healed
After a successful DC 15 Discipline test
At the end of combat, or after a short rest
questions.explanation: A PC can choose to regain consciousness at the end of any of their turns, or when an effect heals them to at least 1 health. If they're at 0, they recover 1 health. NPCs only wake when they recover 1 health.

questions.question: An effect applies a condition to everything in an area that includes a cart and some crates. What happens to the objects?
choices: Each object gains the condition too
Objects generally ignore conditions
Objects take 1d4 damage instead of the condition
The condition fails for every target in the area
questions.explanation: Conditions generally only apply to characters; objects in the area ignore them, though the GM may apply a similar narrative effect when it fits.

questions.question: Which two damage types are NOT reduced by deflect?
choices: Energy and keen
Spirit and vital
Impact and spirit
Vital and energy
questions.explanation: Deflect reduces energy, impact and keen. Spirit damage (usually from Shardblades) and vital damage (poison, suffocation, extreme cold) bypass it.

questions.question: A PC is poisoned or exposed to extreme cold. What type of damage is that by default?
choices: Energy
Impact
Spirit
Vital
questions.explanation: Vital damage covers effects that test your constitution, such as poison, suffocation and extreme cold.

questions.question: How is an injury roll calculated?
choices: d20 + Athletics modifier against DC 15
d20 + deflect + modifiers − 5 per existing injury
d20 − the damage taken by the final blow
2d6 + Strength − 2 per existing injury
questions.explanation: An injury roll isn't a skill test: roll a d20, add your armor's deflect and any relevant ability modifiers, and subtract 5 for each injury you already have. The result can be negative.

questions.question: On the Injury Duration table, what does an injury roll result of 6 to 15 mean?
choices: Flesh wound — lasts until after a long rest
Shallow injury — lasts 1d6 days
Vicious injury — lasts 6d6 days
Permanent injury
questions.explanation: Injury roll results: 16+ flesh wound (until after a long rest); 6–15 shallow (1d6 days); 1–5 vicious (6d6 days); −5 to 0 permanent; −6 or lower death.

questions.question: What injury roll result kills a character?
choices: 0 or lower
−5 or lower
−6 or lower
−10 or lower
questions.explanation: A result of −6 or lower is death; −5 to 0 is a permanent injury.

questions.question: A minor NPC suffers an injury. What happens?
choices: They make an injury roll just like a PC
Defeated; the PC chooses death or Unconscious
They lose half their maximum health instead
They flee the scene and can't return
questions.explanation: Minor NPCs are defeated as soon as they suffer an injury. The PC inflicting it can choose whether they die or fall Unconscious. Major NPCs make injury rolls like PCs.

cite.section: Ch. 9 Adventuring › Minor NPCs and Injuries

questions.question: How does recuperating during downtime affect injury healing?
choices: No effect — injuries heal at a fixed rate
Each recuperating day counts as two
The injury heals after a single day
One injury is removed per full week
questions.explanation: Each downtime day spent on rest and recuperation counts as two days toward healing an injury, so you heal twice as fast.

questions.question: When a PC suffers an injury, who decides what its effect is?
choices: The GM, always — it's part of the narrative
The player, using the table or a custom effect
Always a random d8 roll on the Injury Effects table
The character who dealt the damage that caused it
questions.explanation: The player decides the injury's effects, choosing or rolling (d8) on the Injury Effects table or working out a custom effect with the GM. The player has final say on how an injury affects their character.

questions.question: What does a character recover after a short rest?
choices: All of their lost health and focus
Their recovery die, split between health and focus
Half their maximum health, but no focus
1 focus and 1 health, plus 1 per tier
questions.explanation: A short rest (an uninterrupted hour or more) lets you roll your recovery die and add the result to health, focus or a mix of both.

questions.question: What does a long rest provide?
choices: Recovery die × 2
All lost health and focus, and the Exhausted penalty drops by 1
All health, focus and Investiture, and all injuries heal
All health only
questions.explanation: A long rest (8+ uninterrupted hours) restores all lost health and focus and reduces your Exhausted penalty by 1.

questions.question: During a short rest, a PC chooses Tend to Others instead of recovering. What do the allies they tend get?
choices: Add the tender's Medicine modifier to recovery rolls
Gain an advantage on their recovery die rolls
Recover all of their focus immediately
Shorten one of their injuries by 1 day
questions.explanation: Tend to Others has you forgo your own recovery; the willing allies resting with you add your Medicine modifier to their recovery die rolls.

questions.question: In combat, an effect lasts '1 round'. When does it end?
choices: At the end of the current round
At the end of the affected character's next turn
At the start of the same phase next round
After 6 seconds of real time at the table
questions.explanation: Note which phase the effect began in — fast PC, fast NPC, slow PC or slow NPC. It lasts until the start of that same phase on the next round.

questions.question: How long can a character go without food before suffering ill effects?
choices: 1 day
3 days
A number of days equal to their Willpower
A number of days equal to their Strength
questions.explanation: You can go days equal to your Willpower without food; each further day makes you Exhausted [−1]. Reaching Exhausted [−10] or worse is fatal. Water is harsher: Exhausted [−1] from the first day without it.

questions.question: During a scene with an event track in play, how do the event's slots get filled?
choices: The GM fills one slot at the end of each round
By spending Opportunities or Complications on them
Each failed test fills a slot automatically
A slot fills whenever a character takes an injury
questions.explanation: Opportunities can be spent to fill positive event slots and Complications (spent by the GM) to fill negative ones, giving up their usual effects. The event triggers when the last slot fills.

questions.question: Using the downtime Training activity, how long does it typically take to learn a new expertise, and at what cost?
choices: 5 days at 1 mark per day
10 days at 3 marks per day
20+ days at 5 marks per day
30 days at no cost if a mentor helps
questions.explanation: Training for a new expertise (even a specialist one) usually takes 20+ days at 5 marks per day, and normally needs a relevant skill test. Research, by comparison, is about 10+ days at 3 marks per day.

questions.question: What does the Self-Reflection downtime activity allow?
choices: Swearing an Ideal without completing its goal
A rebuild at the same level; 10+ days at 5 marks/day
Gaining a level after 20 days of reflection
Removing all injuries and Exhausted penalties
questions.explanation: Ten or more days of self-reflection (5 marks/day) let you rebuild your character at your current level with GM approval. Prerequisites still apply, and rewards don't count toward earlier-level prerequisites.

questions.question: A PC in armor with deflect 2 is reduced to 0 health. They already have one injury. They roll a 9 on the injury roll. What happens?
choices: Flesh wound — heals after a long rest
Shallow injury lasting 1d6 days
Vicious injury lasting 6d6 days
Permanent injury
questions.explanation: 9 + 2 (deflect) − 5 (one existing injury) = 6, which is in the 6–15 shallow injury band (1d6 days). They're also Unconscious.

questions.question: An unarmored PC with two existing injuries suffers another and rolls a 7 on the injury roll. What's the outcome?
choices: Shallow injury
Vicious injury
Permanent injury
Death
questions.explanation: 7 − 10 (two existing injuries × 5) = −3, which falls in the −5 to 0 band: a permanent injury.

questions.question: A PC lies Unconscious at 0 health. An enemy spends an attack on them and hits for 4 damage. What happens?
choices: Nothing — they're already at 0 health
They suffer another injury
They die automatically
The pain wakes them, with 1 health
questions.explanation: Each time you take damage while at 0 health, you suffer another injury, with the −5 per existing injury making it more dangerous. (Enemies typically ignore Unconscious characters unless they have a strong reason.)

questions.question: A PC is Exhausted [−2] from travel, then a poison makes them Exhausted [−1]. They roll a Survival test totaling 16. What is the final result?
choices: 16 — only the worst penalty applies
questions.explanation: Exhausted is cumulative: −2 and −1 make a −3 penalty, applied after calculating the result. 16 − 3 = 13.

questions.question: A PC with Speed 3 (30 ft movement) becomes Enhanced [+2 Speed]. What changes?
choices: 40 ft movement and +2 to Speed skills; same defense
40 ft movement and +2 Physical defense
Only movement rises, to 35 ft
Everything Speed affects rises, including defense
questions.explanation: Enhanced Speed 5 uses the 40 ft movement band and adds +2 to Agility, Light Weaponry, Stealth and Thievery tests — but Enhanced never changes defenses.

questions.question: A PC with 30 ft of movement has moved 15 ft when a trap makes them Slowed. How much farther can they move with this Move?
choices: 0 ft
7 ft
8 ft
15 ft
questions.explanation: If you become Slowed mid-movement, halve your remaining movement, rounded up — an exception to the usual round-down rule. Half of 15 is 7.5, rounded up to 8.

questions.question: During the fast PC phase, a PC's ability makes an enemy Disoriented for 1 round. When does it wear off?
choices: At the end of the enemy's next turn
At the start of the fast PC phase on the next round
At the end of this round
At the start of the slow NPC phase this round
questions.explanation: Round-based durations last until the start of the same phase in which they began, on the next round. It began in the fast PC phase, so it ends when the next fast PC phase starts.

questions.question: You've put a positive event, 'Reinforcements Arrive', on the table with Opportunity slots. An enemy NPC rolls a Complication. What can that Complication do?
choices: Nothing — NPCs can't interact with events
It can fill a slot on the PCs' positive event
It must fill a negative event slot
It cancels a filled Opportunity slot
questions.explanation: NPC contributions are inverted: an enemy's Opportunities feed events that are bad for the PCs, and its Complications feed events that are good for them.

questions.question: A PC with Willpower 2 is lost in the wilds with plenty of water but no food for 5 days. What's their condition?
choices: No effect yet
Exhausted [−3]
Exhausted [−5]
Exhausted [−1]
questions.explanation: They can go 2 days (their Willpower) without food. Each day after that adds Exhausted [−1]: days 3, 4 and 5 make Exhausted [−3].

questions.question: After an hour's break between fights, a PC at low health and low focus rolls a 6 on their recovery die. What can they do with it?
choices: 6 health only — focus needs a long rest
6 focus only — health needs a long rest
Any split of the 6 between health and focus
6 health and 6 focus
questions.explanation: After a short rest you add the recovery die result to health, focus or any combination of the two.

questions.question: What's the trade-off between a fast turn and a slow turn?
choices: Fast: 3 actions, no reaction. Slow: 2 plus a reaction
Fast: before enemies, 2 actions. Slow: after, 3
Fast: 2 actions, disadvantage on attacks. Slow: 3
No difference except turn order
questions.explanation: A fast turn goes before any enemies but gives only two actions; a slow turn comes after fast enemies but gives three. Either way you gain a reaction at the start of your turn.

questions.question: What's the order of turn phases in a combat round?
choices: Fast PCs, slow PCs, fast NPCs, slow NPCs
Fast NPCs, fast PCs, slow NPCs, slow PCs
Fast PCs, fast NPCs, slow PCs, slow NPCs
Initiative order by d20 roll
questions.explanation: Each round runs: fast PC turns, fast NPC turns, slow PC turns, slow NPC turns, then the next round begins.

questions.question: When does a character gain reactions in combat?
choices: Only once, at the very start of combat
At combat start (unless Surprised) and each of their turns
Only at the start of a slow turn, never on a fast one
At the end of each round, for every combatant at once
questions.explanation: You gain a reaction when combat starts (unless Surprised), usable before your first turn, then a new one at the start of each of your turns, fast or slow. Each lasts until the start of your next turn or until used.

questions.question: Can a character use the Strike action more than once per turn?
choices: No — named actions are once per turn
Yes, with a different hand; offhand costs 2 focus
Yes, unlimited times with the same weapon
Only on a slow turn, for 1 focus each
questions.explanation: Strike is an exception to the once-per-turn rule, but each Strike must use a different hand and attacking with your offhand costs 2 focus.

questions.question: What does the Brace action do?
choices: Grants +2 deflect until your next turn
Attacks get a disadvantage while you stay behind cover
Lets you ignore the next Shove or Grapple
Makes you immune to Prone until your next turn
questions.explanation: Brace puts you behind cover within 5 feet: attacks from the far side of that cover gain a disadvantage until you attack or move. A Defensive-trait weapon like a shield can act as mobile cover.

questions.question: What does a successful Gain Advantage action give you?
choices: An advantage on all tests vs. that enemy this round
An advantage on your next test vs. them using another skill
An Opportunity on your next test against them
A free Strike against that enemy
questions.explanation: After a successful test (a relevant skill vs. the matching defense), you gain an advantage on your next test against that enemy — but it must use a different skill from the one you used to Gain Advantage.

questions.question: A character is Grappled. Which of these does NOT end the Grapple?
choices: The grappler becomes Unconscious
The target is no longer within the grappler's reach
The grappled character successfully Shoves the grappler
The grappled character takes damage
questions.explanation: Grapple (Athletics vs. Physical) makes the target Restrained until the grappler is Unconscious, chooses to end it, or the target leaves their reach. Successfully Shoving the grappler also ends it. Taking damage doesn't.

questions.question: How often can a character use the Recover action, and what does it do?
choices: Once per round; regain 1 focus
Once per scene; roll your recovery die
Twice per scene; regain all focus
Unlimited; regain 1d4 health each time
questions.explanation: Recover (a two-action activity) lets you roll your recovery die for health and/or focus as if after a short rest. It can be used only once per scene.

questions.question: What does the Aid reaction cost and give?
choices: Free; the ally gets +2 on the test
1 focus; the ally gains an advantage
2 focus; the ally may reroll
1 action; the ally gains an Opportunity
questions.explanation: Before an ally makes a skill test, you can use your reaction and spend 1 focus to grant them an advantage — if you're realistically in position to help.

questions.question: Which statement about the Dodge reaction is correct?
choices: It costs no focus at all, only the reaction itself
1 focus: disadvantage on one attack; not vs. area attacks
Move 5 feet, possibly out of an area attack's zone
Turn an incoming hit into a graze for 2 focus
questions.explanation: Dodge costs your reaction and 1 focus to add a disadvantage to an attack before it's made. It doesn't work on area attacks or attacks with multiple targets — Avoid Danger might help there.

questions.question: What triggers a Reactive Strike, and what does it cost?
choices: An enemy entering your reach; free
An enemy voluntarily leaving your reach; 1 focus
Any enemy moving within 30 feet; 1 action
An enemy attacking an ally; 2 focus
questions.explanation: When an enemy voluntarily leaves your reach, you can use your reaction and spend 1 focus to make a melee weapon attack against their Physical defense. Instant movement like Transportation doesn't trigger it.

questions.question: An attack misses. What option does the attacker have?
choices: None — a miss deals no damage
Spend 1 focus per target to graze for the dice total
Spend an Opportunity to turn it into a hit
Spend 2 focus to reroll the attack
questions.explanation: On a miss you can spend 1 focus per target to graze, dealing damage equal to the damage dice alone. A hit adds your skill modifier to the dice.

questions.question: What does turning a hit into a critical hit do?
choices: Doubles all damage dealt by the attack
Treats all damage dice as rolling their maximum
Adds one extra damage die of the same size
Inflicts an automatic injury on the target
questions.explanation: Spending an Opportunity on a hit makes it a critical hit, maximizing the damage dice against all targets of that attack (the skill modifier is still added as usual).

questions.question: A thrown weapon has range [20/60]. What happens when attacking a target 40 feet away?
choices: Normal attack
The attack gains a disadvantage
The attack can't be made
The attack takes a −5 penalty
questions.explanation: Inside the short range (20 ft) tests are normal; between short and long range (up to 60 ft) they gain a disadvantage; beyond long range you can't attack.

cite.section: Ch. 10 Combat › Long and Short Range

questions.question: A PC attacks where they believe a hidden enemy is but can't sense them. What applies?
choices: The attack automatically misses
The attack has a disadvantage and can't graze
Normal attack, but no damage modifier
The attack gains an advantage because the enemy is unaware
questions.explanation: If you know roughly where a target is but can't sense them, attacks and other physical-effect tests against them gain a disadvantage, and those attacks can't graze.

cite.section: Ch. 10 Combat › Locating and Sensing Targets

questions.question: Does forced movement, like a Shove, trigger Reactive Strikes?
choices: Yes — leaving reach always triggers it
No — forced movement never triggers it
Only if pushed more than 5 feet
Only against Large or bigger characters
questions.explanation: Forced movement ignores the target's movement rate and doesn't trigger Reactive Strike or other abilities that trigger when a character leaves your reach.

questions.question: How much falling damage does a character take?
choices: 1d6 impact per 10 feet, and Prone if damaged
1d10 impact per 10 feet, no other effect
1d6 impact per 5 feet, no other effect
A flat 5 damage per 10 feet, and Prone
questions.explanation: Falling at least 10 feet deals 1d6 impact damage per 10 feet. If you take any damage from the fall, you land Prone.

questions.question: What does a rider need to use their mount's abilities (from its stat block) in combat?
choices: Nothing — mounts take their own separate turn
A riding expertise for that mount; they spend their own resources
A successful Survival test at the start of each round
2 focus per round, paid by the rider to keep control
questions.explanation: With the right riding expertise you can activate the mount's abilities on your turn using your own focus and actions. Without it, the mount takes no actions of its own.

questions.question: An ally Shoves an enemy 5 feet, out of the reach of the PC next to it. The PC still has their reaction and focus. Can they make a Reactive Strike?
choices: Yes, it left their reach
Yes, but with a disadvantage
No — forced movement doesn't trigger Reactive Strike
No — Reactive Strike only works on the PC's own turn
questions.explanation: Reactive Strike needs an enemy to voluntarily leave your reach. Being pushed is forced movement, which never triggers it.

questions.question: An enemy Elsecaller standing next to a PC uses Transportation to vanish and reappear across the room. Can the PC Reactive Strike?
choices: Yes — they left the PC's reach voluntarily
No — instant movement like this can't be targeted
Yes, but the Reactive Strike has a disadvantage
Only if the PC is wielding a reach weapon
questions.explanation: Reactive Strike explicitly can't be used on a character who transports themselves with Transportation or otherwise moves instantaneously.

questions.question: A PC archer has an enemy soldier right next to them but shoots at an enemy officer 30 feet away (within short range). What modifies the attack?
choices: Nothing
A disadvantage, because they're within an enemy's reach
An advantage, because the officer is unaware
The stakes are raised
questions.explanation: A ranged attack made while you're within reach of any enemy gains a disadvantage.

cite.section: Ch. 10 Combat › Ranged Attacks and Reach

questions.question: A PC fires a shortbow at an enemy who is locked in melee, within 5 feet of the PC's ally. The attack misses and the plot die shows a Complication. What can you, the GM, do?
choices: Nothing special — the stakes weren't raised
Spend it to make the shot graze the ally
Spend it to make the PC drop their bow
The ally takes full hit damage automatically
questions.explanation: Ranged attacks against a target within 5 feet of the attacker's ally always raise the stakes. On a miss with a Complication, the GM can spend it so the shot grazes the ally, at no focus cost.

cite.section: Ch. 10 Combat › Ranged Attacks and Reach

questions.question: A PC with a +4 Heavy Weaponry modifier hits with a weapon dealing 1d10 keen damage, rolling a 5. The target's armor has deflect 2. How much damage does the target take?
questions.explanation: A hit deals the damage dice plus the skill modifier: 5 + 4 = 9. Keen damage is reduced by deflect: 9 − 2 = 7.

questions.question: A PC with Light Weaponry +3 attacks with a weapon dealing 2d6, rolls 2 and 4 on the damage dice, and hits. They have an Opportunity and spend it to critically hit. How much damage (before deflect)?
questions.explanation: A critical hit treats all damage dice as their maximum: 2d6 becomes 12. Add the skill modifier for a hit: 12 + 3 = 15.

questions.question: A PC's attack misses. Their damage dice rolled a total of 6, and their skill modifier is +3. They spend 1 focus. What happens?
choices: They graze for 6 damage
They graze for 9 damage
They hit for 9 damage
They graze for 3 damage
questions.explanation: Spending 1 focus on a miss turns it into a graze, which deals only the damage dice total — 6 — without the skill modifier.

questions.question: A PC is shoved off a ledge and falls 30 feet onto stone. What happens?
choices: 1d6 impact damage
3d6 impact damage and they land Prone
3d6 impact damage, no other effect
An automatic injury
questions.explanation: Falling deals 1d6 impact damage per 10 feet — 3d6 for 30 feet — and taking any fall damage leaves you Prone. (They could first try Avoid Danger to catch themselves.)

questions.question: A PC uses Gain Advantage, testing Deduction to read a duelist's footwork, and succeeds. Which of their next tests against that duelist can use the advantage?
choices: Any test against the duelist, even another Deduction test
Their next test vs. the duelist with another skill
Only another Deduction test against the same duelist
Only a test made by one of their allies this round
questions.explanation: The advantage applies to your next test against that enemy using a different skill from the one you used to gain it.

questions.question: Two PCs have taken fast turns. The third PC planned to go slow but, after seeing the situation, wants to go fast now, before the fast NPCs. Is that allowed?
choices: No — fast/slow must be declared at the start of the round
Yes — the choice can be made in the moment and changes each round
Only if they spend 1 focus
Only with a Speed higher than the other PCs
questions.explanation: You choose fast or slow each round, and the decision doesn't need to be made at the start of the round. You can opt in after the other fast PCs have gone.

questions.question: Bandits ambush the party, and you rule two PCs are Surprised. What does that mean for those PCs on the first round?
choices: They skip their first turn entirely
No reaction, no fast turn, one fewer action
A disadvantage on all tests for this round
They begin the combat Prone and Slowed
questions.explanation: Surprised characters lose reactions (and don't gain one at the start of combat or on their turn), can't take a fast turn, and gain one fewer action. The condition is removed after their next turn.

questions.question: On their turn, a PC uses Ready to Strike the first enemy who comes through a door. No enemy comes through before the PC's next turn. What happens to the actions they spent?
choices: They're refunded on the next turn
They're lost
They carry over as a bonus action
The PC can Strike at any target instead
questions.explanation: If the trigger doesn't occur (or you choose not to respond), you don't regain the actions spent on Ready and the prepared action.

questions.question: An enemy Dustbringer targets an area containing a PC with a gout of flame. The PC wants to Dodge. What's the correct ruling?
choices: Dodge works normally for 1 focus
No Dodge; they can try Avoid Danger instead
They automatically take half damage
Dodge works, but costs 2 focus
questions.explanation: Dodge can't be used against area or multi-target attacks. Avoid Danger lets you test Agility against the triggering test's result; on a success you avoid the danger to a reasonable degree, as the GM judges.

questions.question: A PC is knocked Prone. An enemy swordsman and an enemy archer (30 feet away) both attack them. Which attack gains an advantage from the Prone condition?
choices: Both
Only the swordsman's melee attack
Only the archer's ranged attack
Neither
questions.explanation: While Prone, melee attacks against you gain an advantage. The condition doesn't grant ranged attackers an advantage.

questions.question: Playing on a 5-foot grid, a Slowed PC has 5 feet of movement left. Can they move one more square?
choices: Yes — one square always costs 5 feet
No — Slowed, they need 10 feet left
Yes, but only orthogonally
Only with a successful Athletics test
questions.explanation: On a grid you need at least 5 feet of movement left to enter a square, or 10 feet if you're Slowed.

cite.section: Ch. 10 Combat › Variant: Using a Grid (Movement)

questions.question: A PC wants to use an ability that targets 'a character within reach' on themselves. Allowed?
choices: No — abilities only target others
Yes — you are a character
Only with GM approval each time
Only for healing effects
questions.explanation: Since you're a character, an effect targeting 'a character' can target you. Note, though, that you aren't considered your own ally.

questions.question: After a PC succeeds on a social test against an NPC, how much focus must the NPC spend to resist being influenced?
choices: 1 focus, always
2 if reasonably persuasive; 4 if extremely strong
Focus equal to how much the PC beat the DC by
None — they can't resist a successful test
questions.explanation: The GM decides how persuasive the contribution was: reasonably persuasive costs 2 focus to resist, extremely strong costs 4. Some arguments are so compelling the NPC might not resist at all.

questions.question: What happens when an NPC in a conversation is reduced to 0 focus?
choices: They fall Unconscious from the strain
They can no longer resist being influenced
They must attack or leave immediately
They automatically agree to everything
questions.explanation: At 0 focus an NPC is too frustrated or scattered to contribute effectively. They can't resist influence any more and might disengage entirely, generally conceding the point or opening to compromise.

cite.section: Ch. 11 Conversations › Running Out of Focus

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the conversation types the Handbook describes?
choices: Inquiry
Negotiation
Interrogation
Scheme
questions.explanation: The four described conversation types are Inquiry, Negotiation, Scheme and Social. Interrogations would usually be run as an Inquiry.

questions.question: To influence a character in a conversation, what generally sets the DC of your test?
choices: A flat DC 15 for any social test
Their Spiritual or Cognitive defense
Their current focus + 10
Their Physical defense, if they're hostile
questions.explanation: Influence tests generally target the person's Spiritual or Cognitive defense, matching the skill's category (e.g. Persuasion → Spiritual, Intimidation → Cognitive). The GM can adjust it.

questions.question: An effect says it targets 'a character you can influence.' Can the target resist it?
choices: No — mechanical effects can't be resisted
Yes, unless it says otherwise (usually 2 focus)
Only PCs can resist such effects
Only with a successful Discipline test
questions.explanation: Effects targeting a character you can influence can be resisted by that character unless stated otherwise, by spending focus as if it were a social skill test.

questions.question: Which four endeavor types does the Handbook give specific guidance for?
choices: Discovery, Exploration, Mission, Pursuit
Investigation, Travel, Heist, Chase
Discovery, Survival, Infiltration, Pursuit
Exploration, Mission, Negotiation, Siege
questions.explanation: Chapter 12 covers Discovery, Exploration, Mission and Pursuit endeavors, while noting these are just starting points.

questions.question: How does a Discovery endeavor track progress instead of a collective success threshold?
choices: A distance track between pursuer and target
An investigative web of leads and clues
A ticking clock advanced each round
An event track filled with Opportunities
questions.explanation: A Discovery uses an investigative web: the party starts with leads (usually two to four), each opening a line of clues toward the objective. The GM may still track failures.

cite.section: Ch. 12 Endeavors › Discovery Endeavors (No Threshold for Success)

questions.question: In a Pursuit's distance track, what happens when a pursuer fails a test?
choices: The gap widens by 1
The gap closes by 1
Nothing — only successes count
The target escapes immediately
questions.explanation: Pursuer success closes the gap by 1 and failure widens it by 1. For the target, it's the reverse. The chase ends when the gap hits 0 (caught) or the escape distance (escaped).

cite.section: Ch. 12 Endeavors › Special Rule: Closing the Distance

questions.question: What is the 'Against the Odds' special rule?
choices: Once per Exploration, everyone tests vs. a peril
A Mission rule that doubles Complications
A Pursuit rule that forces opposed tests
A once-per-session reroll for the party
questions.explanation: Once per Exploration, the GM can introduce exceptional perils. Each character makes a related test (e.g. Survival, Athletics, Leadership), and those who fail suffer that peril's effect.

cite.section: Ch. 12 Endeavors › Special Rule: Against the Odds

questions.question: In a Mission endeavor, what can the GM do with a Complication a PC rolls?
choices: Nothing special
Spend it to advance the ticking clock
Add 2 to the failure threshold
End the Mission immediately
questions.explanation: Missions use a ticking clock that advances each round. The GM can also spend PC Complications to advance it further, by an amount of their choosing.

cite.section: Ch. 12 Endeavors › Special Rule: The Ticking Clock

questions.question: A stubborn highlady has 4 focus. The PCs make two successful, reasonably persuasive arguments, and she resists both. A third PC then succeeds on a strong Persuasion test. What happens?
choices: She resists again, spending 2 focus
She can't resist at 0 focus
She resists for free because she's stubborn
She ends the conversation immediately
questions.explanation: Each resisted argument cost her 2 focus (4 → 2 → 0). At 0 focus she can't resist influence, so the third success lands, and she'll likely concede or seek a compromise.

cite.section: Ch. 11 Conversations › Running Out of Focus

questions.question: An NPC succeeds on a Persuasion test to convince a PC to abandon their mission. The PC is at 0 focus. What does the player have to do?
choices: Their character must agree to abandon it
Nothing — the player decides how they respond
Make a DC 15 Discipline test to refuse
Take Exhausted [−1] to refuse
questions.explanation: PCs are never forced to choose between spending focus and acting against their story. Even at 0 focus, the player decides how their character responds.

cite.section: Ch. 11 Conversations › Player Characters and Influence

questions.question: In a Negotiation, a merchant NPC rolls Persuasion to talk a PC into paying a 'danger commission.' What sets the DC?
choices: The PC's Cognitive defense
The PC's Spiritual defense
The PC's Persuasion result in an opposed test, always
DC 15
questions.explanation: Persuasion is a Presence (spiritual) skill, so an NPC persuading a PC tests against the PC's Spiritual defense, just as the Handbook's example conversation shows.

questions.question: In a Pursuit with an escape distance of 6, the current distance is 2. A pursuing PC succeeds on an Agility test, then the fleeing target fails its Stealth test. What's the result?
choices: Distance 2 — they cancel out
Distance 0 — the target is caught
Distance 4
Distance 1
questions.explanation: A pursuer's success closes the gap by 1 (2 → 1), and a target's failure also closes it by 1 (1 → 0). At 0 the target is caught.

cite.section: Ch. 12 Endeavors › Special Rule: Closing the Distance

questions.question: During an endeavor to cross a flooded canyon, a Windrunner simply Lashes the party across. Do you need a test?
choices: Yes — every contribution needs a test
Not necessarily; the GM can just add a success
Yes, a DC 20 Gravitation test
No, and the endeavor ends in automatic success
questions.explanation: Some abilities, especially surges, make demonstrable progress without needing a test; the GM may simply add a success toward the threshold.

questions.question: A party hits the failure threshold in a Discovery endeavor but wants to propose who stole the schematics anyway. What rule covers this?
choices: None — the Discovery simply fails
Betting on a Hunch
Reroll the last failed test with an advantage
Pay 5 marks a day to keep researching
questions.explanation: Betting on a Hunch lets the group make an educated guess after failing. A correct guess counts as success; a wrong one feeds story twists and eventual consequences.

cite.section: Ch. 12 Endeavors › Special Rule: Betting on a Hunch

questions.question: During an Exploration through a region where a PC's powerful patron holds sway, the PC wants to secure safe passage through a checkpoint. What can you do as GM?
choices: Require a DC 20 Persuasion test with a disadvantage
Grant an automatic success on that test
Make them spend Investiture for safe passage
Nothing — patrons don't apply in endeavors
questions.explanation: In an Exploration, a relevant expertise or reward (like a patron with regional influence) can grant automatic success on certain tests, at the GM's discretion.

questions.question: What does choosing a First Ideal key talent immediately grant?
choices: Both of the order's surges, plus a Shardblade
Investiture, the three Stormlight actions and an Ideal goal
Only a spren companion who follows them everywhere
Full Radiant status and the Empowered condition
questions.explanation: The First Ideal talent (level 2+) immediately unlocks Investiture and the three Stormlight actions and grants the goal 'Speak the First Ideal.' The order's two surges come only once that goal is completed.

cite.section: Ch. 5 Radiant Paths › Choosing a First Ideal Talent

questions.question: How much Investiture does a Radiant usually have at the start of a scene?
choices: 0 — they must Breathe Stormlight first
Full — or just 1 if they start Surprised
Half their maximum, rounded down
2, regardless of their maximum
questions.explanation: It's assumed a Radiant instinctively breathed in Stormlight beforehand, so they start full. A Radiant who starts the scene Surprised has only 1 Investiture.

questions.question: When can the GM assume a Radiant has enough infused spheres without tracking them?
choices: Always — Stormlight is never worth tracking
When they carry marks worth 3× their Investiture
When they carry at least one infused broam
Only while they're within the walls of Urithiru
questions.explanation: If a Radiant carries marks equal to at least three times their Investiture total (and highstorms are accessible), assume they have enough Stormlight. Track spheres only when the story makes it matter.

questions.question: What does the Regenerate action do?
choices: Spend 2 Investiture to heal 2d6 health
1 Investiture: heal 1d6 + tier, even Unconscious
Spend 1 focus to heal 1d4 health
Spend 1 Investiture to heal one injury
questions.explanation: Regenerate is a free action: spend 1 Investiture to recover 1d6 + your tier in health. It works even while you're Unconscious or otherwise unable to act.

questions.question: What does the Enhance Stormlight action grant for 1 Investiture?
choices: +1 Strength and +1 Speed until the end of next turn
+2 to any one attribute for the whole scene
+1 deflect until the end of the scene
An advantage on your next attack test
questions.explanation: Enhance makes you Enhanced [Strength +1] and [Speed +1] until the end of your next turn. You can keep paying 1 Investiture at the end of each turn to maintain it.

questions.question: How many milestone boxes must be marked on an Ideal goal before the Radiant can speak those Words?
choices: One
Two
Three
Five
questions.explanation: Each Ideal goal has three milestone boxes, marked for dramatic, philosophy-aligned actions. Once all three are marked, the player and GM can set up the moment to speak the Words.

cite.section: Ch. 5 Radiant Paths › Ideals and Goals

questions.question: What happens the first time a Radiant acts against their Ideals?
choices: They lose their highest Ideal
Nothing — mistakes can be forgiven
Their spren dies
They lose all Investiture
questions.explanation: The first infraction has no effect. A second before demonstrably advancing their Ideals costs their highest Ideal and dependent talents, and further breaches strip more.

cite.section: Ch. 5 Radiant Paths › Forsaking Your Ideals

questions.question: What does a squire gain while within range of their Radiant?
choices: Access to every one of the Radiant's talents
Investiture 2 and the Stormlight actions within 50 miles
A Shardblade of their own, summoned at will
Nothing at all until they bond their own spren
questions.explanation: Within 50 miles of their Radiant (who must have the Take Squire talent, available after the Third Ideal), a squire can draw Stormlight with Investiture max 2 and use Breathe Stormlight, Enhance and Regenerate. The Radiant may also grant one or both surges at 1 rank.

questions.question: Which two surges does the Windrunner order wield?
choices: Adhesion and Gravitation
Gravitation and Division
Adhesion and Tension
Transportation and Gravitation
questions.explanation: Windrunners (honorspren) wield Adhesion and Gravitation. Skybreakers have Division and Gravitation; Bondsmiths have Adhesion and Tension.

cite.section: Ch. 5 Radiant Paths › Radiant Orders table

questions.question: Which order wields Illumination and Transformation?
choices: Truthwatchers
Elsecallers
Lightweavers
Willshapers
questions.explanation: Lightweavers (Cryptics) wield Illumination and Transformation. Truthwatchers have Illumination and Progression; Elsecallers have Transformation and Transportation.

cite.section: Ch. 5 Radiant Paths › Radiant Orders table

questions.question: How far can a newly bonded spren move from their Radiant before temporarily losing sapience?
choices: 5 feet, the reach of an arm
30 feet, expandable by talent
100 feet, or 200 in Shadesmar
1 mile, the range of a spanreed
questions.explanation: Spren bond range starts at 30 feet; beyond it a newly bonded spren temporarily loses sapience. The Deepened Bond talent increases the range.

questions.question: A Radiant has 3 ranks in a surge skill. What are their surge die size and surge size?
choices: d6, Medium (5 ft)
d8, Large (10 ft)
d10, Huge (15 ft)
d8, Medium (5 ft)
questions.explanation: Surge Scaling: 1 rank d4/Small, 2 d6/Medium, 3 d8/Large (10 ft), 4 d10/Huge, 5 d12/Gargantuan.

questions.question: How does an infused surge effect use up its Investiture?
choices: All at once, when the surge is first used
1 at the start of each of your turns
1 per minute, regardless of combat
It never runs out while you're conscious
questions.explanation: Surges usually expend 1 Investiture at the start of each of your turns, even if you're Unconscious. An object infused with 2 Investiture lasts two rounds.

questions.question: Outside combat, roughly how long does one 'round' of a surge's Investiture last during a conversation?
choices: About 10 seconds
About one minute
About 10 minutes
About one hour
questions.explanation: Combat: once per 10-second round. Conversation: about once per minute. Endeavor: 1–10 minutes depending on the endeavor. Outside scenes: about every 10 minutes.

questions.question: A tier 2 Radiant is knocked Unconscious at 0 health but still has 3 Investiture. What can they do?
choices: Nothing until someone else heals them
Regenerate for 1 Investiture: 1d6 + 2 health
Use Enhance to get back on their feet
Breathe Stormlight, but they can't Regenerate
questions.explanation: Regenerate is usable while Unconscious: 1 Investiture recovers 1d6 + tier (2) health. They can then choose to wake. Breathe Stormlight also works while Unconscious.

questions.question: Assassins ambush a party, and the party's Skybreaker (max Investiture 5) is Surprised. How much Investiture does the Skybreaker start the combat with?
questions.explanation: Radiants normally start scenes full, but a Radiant who starts the scene Surprised has only 1 Investiture — enough to maintain ongoing powers.

questions.question: A Radiant with 2 ranks in Adhesion wants to infuse a 10-foot-long cart. Can they?
choices: Yes, if they infuse 2 Investiture
No — 2 ranks only reaches Medium (5 ft)
Yes, but the test has a disadvantage
Only if they also spend 2 focus
questions.explanation: Surge size scales with ranks: 2 ranks is Medium (5 ft). Unless specified otherwise, you can't infuse an object with any dimension beyond your surge size.

questions.question: A Radiant infuses a door with 3 Investiture to keep it sealed, then fights in the next room. Absent other effects, how long does the infusion last?
choices: Until the end of the scene
Three rounds
One round
Until the Radiant falls Unconscious
questions.explanation: An infusion expends 1 Investiture at the start of each of your turns, so 3 infused Investiture lasts three rounds. The Radiant can add more at the start of a turn if within range. (If the surge isn't relevant to the new scene, the GM may track it more loosely.)

questions.question: A Windrunner abandons a defenseless village in a way that clearly breaks their Ideals. It's the second time since they last advanced their Ideals. What happens?
choices: Nothing — only the first breach matters
They lose their highest Ideal and its talents
They lose all Radiant abilities immediately
Their spren dies on the spot
questions.explanation: The first breach is forgiven. A second, before demonstrably advancing their Ideals, weakens the bond: they lose their highest Ideal and talents that require it. They can repair the bond by genuinely rededicating themselves.

cite.section: Ch. 5 Radiant Paths › Forsaking Your Ideals

questions.question: How is the human Rosharan calendar structured?
choices: 365 days; 12 months of 30 days, plus 5 feast days
500 days; 10 months of 10 five-day weeks
400 days; 10 months, each of 40 days
500 days; 5 months, each of 100 days
questions.explanation: The Rosharan year has 500 days: ten months, each of ten weeks, each of five days. Days are 20 hours long.

questions.question: What happens on Lightday, the Rosharan new year in the middle of the Weeping?
choices: It's always a clear, calm day across Roshar
Clear in even years; a highstorm in odd years
The Everstorm always arrives on Lightday
Every sphere on Roshar goes dun until dawn
questions.explanation: The Weeping's four weeks of rain are interrupted by Lightday: a clear day in even-numbered years, a highstorm in odd-numbered years.

questions.question: What is Midpeace?
choices: A yearly truce between Alethkar and Jah Keved
Four weeks at midyear with no highstorms
The hour of night when no moons are visible
A listener festival held at the Lull
questions.explanation: Midpeace falls halfway between Weepings: four weeks without highstorms.

questions.question: How do sphere denominations convert?
choices: 1 mark = 10 chips; 1 broam = 10 marks
1 mark = 5 chips; 1 broam = 4 marks (20 chips)
1 mark = 4 chips; 1 broam = 5 marks
1 broam = 2 marks = 8 chips
questions.explanation: Spheres come as chips, marks and broams: one mark is five chips, and one broam is four marks (twenty chips).

questions.question: Which gem type makes the most valuable spheres, and which the least?
choices: Diamond most, emerald least
Emerald most, diamond least
Ruby most, garnet least
Sapphire most, topaz least
questions.explanation: Value follows a gem's usefulness in Soulcasting. Emerald is top (an emerald mark is worth 50 diamond marks) and diamond is lowest, so the game prices everything in diamond marks ('clearmarks').

questions.question: Which part of a highstorm is generally considered the most dangerous?
choices: The riddens
The stormwall
The centerbeat
The main body
questions.explanation: The stormwall at the front carries tempestuous winds, debris and torrential rain. The main body is less deadly, and the riddens at the end bring light rain and mild wind.

questions.question: Why was the Everstorm's first arrival so devastating to human settlements?
choices: It carried far more crem than highstorms
It blows west to east, hitting unprotected sides
It only ever strikes at night
It drains the Stormlight from all spheres
questions.explanation: Highstorms blow east to west, so buildings have reinforced stormward (eastern) sides. The Everstorm moves west to east, hitting the vulnerable leeward sides.

questions.question: Which describes the Everstorm?
choices: White clouds and blue lightning; extra crem
Black clouds, red lightning, no stormwall or crem
A stationary storm over the Shattered Plains
A highstorm that only comes during the Weeping
questions.explanation: Driven by Odium, the Everstorm has black clouds and red lightning, lacks a stormwall and crem, and usually comes every nine days — though Odium can speed or stall it.

questions.question: Roughly how long can each of these hold Stormlight: a person, a sphere, a perfect gemstone?
choices: Hours; weeks; years
Minutes; days; indefinitely
Seconds; hours; days
Days; months; indefinitely
questions.explanation: Stormlight leaks out over time: people hold it for minutes, spheres for days, larger gems longer, and rare perfect gemstones indefinitely.

questions.question: Why can the largest greatshells move at all despite their immense weight?
choices: They live only in water
They form symbiotic bonds with luckspren
They draw Stormlight from highstorms
Cultivation granted them Shardplate
questions.explanation: Greatshells bond with luckspren; without these bonds, the largest would be crushed by their own weight.

questions.question: Which Radiant order bonds lightspren, also called Reachers?
choices: Windrunners
Willshapers
Lightweavers
Truthwatchers
questions.explanation: Lightspren (Reachers) grant surges to Willshapers. Lightweavers bond Cryptics (liespren); Truthwatchers bond mistspren.

questions.question: The Sibling, the Bondsmith spren who manifests as Urithiru, is a Splinter of which Shard(s)?
choices: Honor alone
Cultivation alone
Both Honor and Cultivation
Odium alone
questions.explanation: The Sibling is a Splinter of both Honor and Cultivation. The Stormfather is of Honor, and the Nightwatcher is of Cultivation.
